reports.feedback: I've really enjoyed this project! It's given me the opportunity to expand my hardware design skills to beyond RTL. Being able to go through a whole synthesis run, doing gate level simulations all the way to getting back a physical chip. It's all been a wild and wonderful journey!

Tiny Tapeout is something that I started look for back in 2014 when I started undergrad. Now that I'm completing my PhD and Tiny Tapeout exists, it's still a great learning opportunity, and one that I've directed as many undergrads as I can towards. In the 80s they wanted to bring silicon design to the high-school level and tools like magic were optimized to run on the underpowered computers that high schools could conceivably have, Tiny Tapeout is the first program that has made that remotely plausible and I cannot wait to see more.

It is extremely satisfying to have my design baked into physical hardware and working as expected. No flashing of microcontroller firmware, computer software or FPGA bitstream. Just fixed electronic circuits doing your bidding. I have certainly gained a better appreciation of the chip design process.
Excited to see this working so well (despite old OpenLane synth bug), and TT04 Demo Board is a dream to work with!

Tiny Tapeout has inspired me to learn more about hardware design.  I've learnt a lot about how ASICs work, how to use the Open Source design tools, and how to create designs that take best advantage of the constraints.
It's amazing to be able to design my own processor and have it manufactured in silicon for a price that's affordable as a hobbyist!

As a hobbyist, being able to get a physical chip manufactured with less hassle than programming some FPGAs is incredible. It is also very addicting, I'm already thinking about what todo do for my 4th submission.

Initial test of design using a logic analyzer connected to the IO pins.
an SPI data analyzer was used on (MOSI -> uo[0], CS -> uo[1], SCK -> uo[2]) 8-bit packets were used for analysis (matching the register width of the scan chain output). Other logic analyzer pins were attached to the `refclk` (generated by the rpi pico with the command `tt.pins.ui_in0.pwm(32768)` ), `use_refclk`, `fast_set`, `hours_set`, and `minutes_set`. All pins other than the `refclk` signal were controlled via the commander interface.
When no inputs are set the clock runs off the system clock divided to produce correct ticks. The display updates at 1Hz. When the `minutes_set` button is "pressed" the clock enters time-set mode and the clock updates at ~2Hz and the minutes values are updated while the seconds and hours remain constant. Likewise for the `hours_set` button. If both are pressed together then the seconds are reset to zero.
Similarly, if `fast_set` was asserted the time is updated at a rate of ~5Hz.
When `use_refclk` was selected and an appropriate signal was provided, the clock worked without the need for the system clock divider.

Tested PAL using different configurations and programming rates using a PIO controller up to 125MHz PIO speed (31.25MHz PAL config CLK rate).  

Testing was done by implemening a 3-bit state machine with Python saving the current "state" and the PAL decoding the state and 5-bit inputs to determine 1) the next state, 2) a "valid detection" bit and 3) a 'done' bit.   Data is fed to the PAL in modified 5-bit ASCII (uppercase letters only and a few punctuation).  The programmed FSM is designed to detect a specific string like "HELLO WORLD", "DON'T PANIC", etc.  with the 3-bit state tracking 0-7 then rolling back to 0 mid-string.

Instructions and code are provided for generating your own string tests.  The generation code consists of a modified version Matthias Musch's awesome bit generation Python code wrapped by an FSM parser to generate input boolean equations to his generator.

The problem doesn't lie in the register file itself but in an "impedance" mismatch when changing the RISC-V core to use it. First off the check for `zero` register access is in the wrong pipeline level. This doesn't actually cause any issue in practice since that value is stable before/after.  But another sneaky difference between the previous code and the register file macro is the behavior when reading/writing the same register in the same cycle. The Register File explicitely performs a write-before-read (i.e. read returns the new value). But this CPU core depends on a read-before-write (i.e. read return the old value) in one specific case : When performing AMO (Atomic Memory Operations) where Rd == Rs2. There are 268 such instruction in the default "Image" to boot linux and cause it to crash during boot.

While all elements of the design appear to be functional, the slowest speed (n_stages[3:0] = 12 through15 which yield 25 stages) is nearly 50 MHz, so a spectrum analyzer and H-field probe were used to check most of the stage settings by looking at the oscillator harmonics. The probe is probably picking up the IO current(s) and not the oscillator directly.
The frequency vs number of stages fairly closely follows 1/(2*N*tpd) for a tpd ≈ 401 ps, which shows the number of stages selection is working. It is also possible to set the initial states to faster modes/frequencies that persist indefinitely (tested with 25 stages and an input pattern of hAA h55 hAA h55 in big endian byte order) which shows that the FIFO and enable are working. The hold feature also works and resolves any fast modes. Testing different starting patterns with 25 stages showed that multiple edges closer than 6 inverters resolved quickly to the fundamental mode. The AAs and 55s pattern was the shortest that persisted indefinitely, though other patterns did show delay between enabling and changing logic levels on the analyzer vs. a clean starting state.
In hindsight I should have added more stages and plan to do that if this design is iterated. The core concern about ring oscillators having fast modes is validated.

CORDIC peripheral on TinyQV works. Tested sine and cosine for angles from 0 to 2π. Check the results and the MicroPython script [here](https://gist.github.com/rohanverma94/89673a98bc9b98547edd95e2b623e5a7).

- Problem: the core only converges within ±99.9° (sum of micro-rotations, Σatan(2⁻ⁱ)). Push it past that and the rotator diverges into garbage.
- Fix: fold every angle into [-π/2, π/2], track the quadrant, adjust signs accordingly.
- Result: accurate across the whole range. RMS error ~0.23e-3, mean absolute error ~0.16e-3.
- Worst case lands right at the fold boundaries (±90°), where the input angle is largest so the rotator runs the most micro-rotations and piles up the most residual, hence peak error 0.57e-3 at 168.75°/348.75°.
